rows.stem: If the mean and the mode of a distribution are 15 and 18 respectively, then the median of the distribution is :
rows.solution:
Use the empirical relation Mode \(= 3\,\)Median \(- 2\,\)Mean: \(18 = 3\,\)Median \(- 2 \times 15\), so \(3\,\)Median \(= 48\) and Median \(= 16\).

This is option (C) \(16\).

rows.subtopic: Probability with Cards, Dice and Coins
rows.stem: One card is drawn at random from a well shuffled pack of 52 playing cards. The probability that the drawn card is a queen, is :
rows.solution:
A pack of 52 cards has 4 queens, so \(P(\text{queen}) = \dfrac{4}{52}\) (that is, \(\dfrac{1}{13}\)).

This is option (B) \(\dfrac{4}{52}\).

rows.stem: PQ is tangent to a circle centered at O. If the radius of the circle is 5 cm, then the length of the tangent PQ is :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the angle OPQ = 30 degrees is given only in the drawing of the circle with centre O, the radius OQ to the point of contact Q and the line OP to the external point P. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
From the figure, Q is the point of contact and \(\angle OPQ = 30^\circ\). The radius OQ is perpendicular to the tangent PQ, so triangle OQP is right-angled at Q.

\(\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{OQ}{PQ}\), so \(PQ = \dfrac{5}{1/\sqrt{3}} = 5\sqrt{3}\) cm, which is option (A) \(5\sqrt{3}\) cm.

rows.stem: If \(\sec\theta - \tan\theta = \dfrac{1}{3}\), then the value of \((\sec\theta + \tan\theta)\) is :
A quadratic equation whose roots are \((3 - \sqrt{2})\) and \((3 + \sqrt{2})\) is :
rows.solution:
The sum of the roots is \((3 - \sqrt{2}) + (3 + \sqrt{2}) = 6\) and the product is \((3 - \sqrt{2})(3 + \sqrt{2}) = 9 - 2 = 7\).

The equation is \(x^2 - 6x + 7 = 0\), which is option (A) \(x^2 - 6x + 7 = 0\).

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.stem: The solution of the pair of equations \(x + y = a + b\) and \(ax - by = a^2 - b^2\) is :
rows.solution:
Multiply \(x + y = a + b\) by b: \(bx + by = ab + b^2\). Adding this to \(ax - by = a^2 - b^2\) gives \((a + b)x = a^2 + ab = a(a + b)\), so \(x = a\) (taking \(a + b \neq 0\)).

Then \(y = (a + b) - a = b\). (Check: \(a \cdot a - b \cdot b = a^2 - b^2\).)

This is option (C) \(x = a, y = b\).

rows.subtopic: HCF and LCM by Prime Factorisation
rows.stem: Find the greatest 3-digit number which is divisible by 18, 24 and 36.
rows.solution:
A number divisible by each of 18, 24 and 36 is a multiple of their LCM.

\(18 = 2 \times 3^2\), \(24 = 2^3 \times 3\), \(36 = 2^2 \times 3^2\), so LCM \(= 2^3 \times 3^2 = 72\).

The greatest 3-digit number is 999, and \(999 = 72 \times 13 + 63\). So the greatest 3-digit multiple of 72 is \(999 - 63 = 72 \times 13 = 936\).

The required number is 936.

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.stem: A fraction becomes \(\dfrac{1}{3}\) when 1 is subtracted from the numerator. It becomes \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) when 8 is added to the denominator. Find the fraction.
rows.solution:
Let the fraction be \(\dfrac{x}{y}\).

\(\dfrac{x - 1}{y} = \dfrac{1}{3}\), so \(3x - 3 = y\), that is \(3x - y = 3\) ... (i)

\(\dfrac{x}{y + 8} = \dfrac{1}{4}\), so \(4x = y + 8\), that is \(4x - y = 8\) ... (ii)

Subtracting (i) from (ii): \(x = 5\). Then from (i), \(y = 15 - 3 = 12\).

The fraction is \(\dfrac{5}{12}\). (Check: \(\dfrac{5 - 1}{12} = \dfrac{1}{3}\) and \(\dfrac{5}{12 + 8} = \dfrac{1}{4}\).)

rows.subtopic: Sum of First n Terms of an AP
rows.stem: Find the common difference of an A.P. whose first term is 8, the last term is 65 and the sum of all its terms is 730.
rows.solution:
Here \(a = 8\), the last term \(l = 65\) and \(S_n = 730\).

\(S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}(a + l)\), so \(730 = \dfrac{n}{2}(8 + 65) = \dfrac{73n}{2}\), giving \(n = \dfrac{730 \times 2}{73} = 20\).

The last term is the 20th term: \(l = a + 19d\), so \(65 = 8 + 19d\), \(19d = 57\) and \(d = 3\).

The common difference is 3. (The marking scheme prints this step as \(65 = 18 + 19d\), a misprint for 8; its \(d = 3\) is right.)

rows.stem: Two pillars are standing on either side of a 80 m wide road. Height of one pillar is 20 m more than the height of the other pillar. From a point on the road between the pillars, the angle of elevation of the higher pillar is \(60^\circ\), whereas that of the other pillar is \(30^\circ\). Find the position of the point between the pillars and the height of each pillar. (Use \(\sqrt{3} = 1{\cdot}73\))
rows.solution:
Let PQ be the higher pillar and RS the other, standing at the two edges of the road, so \(PR = 80\) m. Let the height of RS be h m, so the height of PQ is \((h + 20)\) m. Let A be the point on the road, with \(PA = x\) m and \(AR = (80 - x)\) m. The elevation of Q from A is \(60^\circ\) and that of S is \(30^\circ\).

In right triangle QPA: \(\tan 60^\circ = \dfrac{h + 20}{x} = \sqrt{3}\), so \(h + 20 = \sqrt{3}\,x\) ... (i)

In right triangle SRA: \(\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{h}{80 - x} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), so \(\sqrt{3}\,h = 80 - x\) ... (ii)

From (i), \(h = \sqrt{3}\,x - 20\). Putting this in (ii): \(3x - 20\sqrt{3} = 80 - x\), so \(4x = 80 + 20\sqrt{3}\) and \(x = 20 + 5\sqrt{3} = 20 + 5 \times 1{\cdot}73 = 28{\cdot}65\).

So the point is \(28{\cdot}65\) m from the foot of the higher pillar and \(80 - 28{\cdot}65 = 51{\cdot}35\) m from the foot of the other.

Then \(h = \sqrt{3}(20 + 5\sqrt{3}) - 20 = 20\sqrt{3} - 5 = 34{\cdot}6 - 5 = 29{\cdot}6\) m.

The shorter pillar is about \(29{\cdot}6\) m high and the higher pillar about \(49{\cdot}6\) m high.

The marking scheme gives \(29{\cdot}56\) m and \(49{\cdot}56\) m, from putting the rounded \(x = 28{\cdot}65\) back into (i): \(1{\cdot}73 \times 28{\cdot}65 - 20 = 29{\cdot}56\). The small difference comes only from rounding \(\sqrt{3}\) at different steps.
